topics.title: Mappings and Relations
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: Use arrow diagrams/mappings to represent relations and functions. (k, u)
Identify domain and range of a mapping. (k, u)
Describe and distinguish between function and non-function mapping. (u, s)

body.text: A mapping connects each member of one set (the domain) to a member of another set (the range) using an arrow diagram. The set of starting values is the domain; the set of values they map to is the range.
Consider the mapping "add 3" from the set {5, 7, 8, 10} to another set. Applying the rule: 5 -> 8, 7 -> 10, 8 -> 11, 10 -> 13. The domain is {5, 7, 8, 10} and the range is {8, 10, 11, 13}.

A mapping is a function only if every member of the domain maps to exactly one member of the range. "Add 3" is a function, because each input gives a single output. A mapping where one input arrows to two different outputs (for example, both 4 and -4 mapping from 16 under "square root") is not a function — it is a one-to-many relation.

Mappings can be one-to-one (each domain value has its own range value, e.g. "add 3"), many-to-one (several domain values share a range value, e.g. "square", since both 2 and -2 map to 4), or one-to-many (not a function). Checking which is which comes down to counting how many arrows leave and arrive at each point.
